content: Bladder neck needle suspension is a surgical procedure traditionally employed to address moderate to severe stress urinary incontinence (SUI) in women. Stress urinary incontinence is a condition that significantly impacts the quality of life and imposes both health and economic burdens on affected individuals and society. Approximately one-third of adult women experience some form of urinary incontinence, with a substantial proportion of these cases classified as moderate or severe. The objective of this analysis was to evaluate the effectiveness of bladder neck needle suspension in treating stress or mixed urinary incontinence, particularly in comparison to other available management options. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted using the Cochrane Incontinence Group Specialised Register, which includes trials identified from databases such as the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (ICTRP). The search also involved handsearching journals, conference proceedings, and reference lists of relevant articles, with the most recent search performed on November 12, 2014. The review included randomized or quasi-randomized trials that investigated the use of needle suspension for urinary incontinence. Data extraction and trial assessment were conducted independently by at least two authors, and additional information was obtained from two trial investigators. A total of 10 trials were identified, involving 375 women who underwent six different types of needle suspension procedures and 489 women who received alternative interventions. The findings revealed that needle suspension was more likely to fail compared to open abdominal retropubic suspension. Specifically, the subjective failure rate after the first year was higher in the needle suspension group (29%, or 91 out of 313 women) compared to the open abdominal retropubic suspension group (16%, or 47 out of 297 women). The calculated risk ratio (RR) was 2.00, with a 95% confidence interval (CI) of 1.47 to 2.72. However, there was no significant difference in peri-operative complications between the two groups (23% in the needle suspension group versus 16% in the open abdominal retropubic suspension group; RR 1.44, 95% CI 0.73 to 2.83). The observed differences in failure rates were consistent among women with primary incontinence as well as those with recurrent incontinence following failed primary surgeries. When compared to anterior vaginal repair, needle suspension appeared to have similar effectiveness, with failure rates of 32% (50 out of 156 women) and 35% (64 out of 181 women), respectively. The risk ratio for this comparison was 0.86 (95% CI 0.64 to 1.16). However, there was limited information available regarding morbidity associated with these procedures. Data comparing needle suspension to suburethral sling procedures were inconclusive due to the small and atypical population studied. Furthermore, no trials were identified that compared needle suspension with conservative management, peri-urethral injections, sham surgery, or laparoscopic surgery. In conclusion, bladder neck needle suspension appears to be less effective than open abdominal retropubic suspension for the treatment of both primary and secondary urodynamic stress incontinence, as evidenced by lower cure rates in the reviewed trials. However, the reliability of this conclusion is limited by the small size and poor quality of the included trials. There was insufficient evidence to draw reliable comparisons between needle suspension and suburethral sling operations. While cure rates were similar between needle suspension and anterior vaginal repair, the data were inadequate to provide definitive conclusions regarding effectiveness or morbidity. Additionally, no cost-effectiveness studies were identified to compare bladder neck needle suspension with other surgical options.
